item.title: Policy Management
item.description: What is a Speedle policy? The Policy Management Service (PMS) manages services, authorization policies, role policies and custom functions. A policy store persists those objects using a registered storage backend. Services and authorization policies A service scopes its policies. An authorization policy grants or denies a principal permission to perform an action on a resource, optionally subject to a condition. Except for global role policies, policies do not automatically apply in another service.

item.title: Usecases
item.description: Application specific policies Alex Chan is a developer who is implementing a simple application with golang. His application requires Authorization and he doesn’t want to re-invent the wheel. Alex can use an open source choice like Speedle for Authorization. Centalized policy enforcement and management Jin Chen is a security manager of multinational company. His team monitor dozens of internal systems. Different systems use different authorization mechanisms, different policy languages. They are eager to find a solution to manage all these systems efficiently.

item.title: Global Policy
item.description: When should a role be global? Ordinary roles are scoped to a service. When several services share a role assignment, define the assignment in the specially named global service and use that role in each service’s own authorization policies. Only global role policies are supported. A global role assignment does not itself grant every operation; each ordinary service still defines its permissions. Global authorization policies are not supported. Before running the examples Build .

item.title: Policy Diagnosis
item.description: What does diagnosis show? Diagnose explains an authorization evaluation: decision, reason, effective roles, attributes, and the policies examined. It accepts the same request context as IsAllowed; REST uses /authz-check/v1/diagnose, and both Go/gRPC use Diagnose. Diagnosis exposes policy definitions and request context. Restrict it to trusted operators using the API security controls; it is not a public debugging endpoint. Before running the examples Build ./bin/spctl, ./bin/speedle-pms and ./bin/speedle-ads using the quick start.

item.title: Policy Discovery
item.description: What can discover mode do? * Help you discover existing authorization requests The is-allowed API endpoint and the discover API endpoint use the same request and response format. When you replace is-allowed with discover in the URL of the API, each authorization request that is returned shows WHO carries out WHAT action on WHICH resource. Discover mode does not evaluate the authorization decision; it simply records the authorization decision requests, along with the actions and the resources protected, and returns “is-allowed=true”.

item.title: SPDL - Speedle Policy Definition Language
item.description: Syntax Keywords grant, deny, user, group, entity, role, from, on, if and in have special meanings in their syntax positions. Statement keywords are case-insensitive. In conditions, use in or IN; function names are case-sensitive. Principal, action and resource names are also case-sensitive. The current parser accepts keyword-like names in some name positions, so a blanket prohibition is not a validation rule. Prefer unambiguous names for review and client interoperability.

item.title: Why Speedle?
item.description: What and Why? Thoughts: Authz is not a new concept. Been using it in software since the dawn of time. Various systems have sprung up with their own little authz solutions. k8s, istio, various IAMs. One may have been using something else for their on premise applications. As folks move to hybrid models / workloads / cloud vendors - how does one keep track of the policies and manage identity as it flows across - these various systems.

item.title: Architecture
item.description: Modules Speedle is an authorization engine with three main components: Policy Management Service (PMS) manages services, authorization policies, role policies and custom functions. Policy repository persists those objects using a registered store such as file, etcd or MongoDB. Authorization Decision Service (ADS) evaluates a subject, resource, action and trusted attributes against the applicable policies. The historical diagram labels the decision component ARS; this is the component called ADS in current documentation and APIs.

item.title: Quick Start
item.description: Try Speedle in the Playground first You can try Speedle’s basic features before installing anything. Open the Playground to edit SPDL policies, set a user, resource and action, and see real Allow/Deny decisions entirely in your browser. No Go installation or running server is required. Continue below when you are ready to build and run Speedle locally. Prerequisites Use Linux or macOS with Bash, Git, curl and Go 1.26.3 or newer.

item.title: RBAC: role-based access control
item.description: How RBAC works in Speedle Role-based access control (RBAC) separates role assignments from permissions. A Speedle role policy assigns a role to a user, group or another role. An authorization policy grants a role permission to perform an action on a resource. The evaluator resolves the applicable roles when answering the request. This is useful when many people share a job function: changing a reader’s permissions updates one authorization policy rather than every user’s grants.

item.title: Speedle embedded mode
item.description: What is embedded mode? An embedded Go application evaluates policies in its own process. It still supplies trusted identities and attributes and enforces the returned decision. Try the Playground first to explore policy semantics without a server. Supported configurations Use Go 1.26 or later, as required by the current go.mod. Within your own application module, add a dependency with go get github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus@<reviewed-tag-or-commit> after go mod init; replace the placeholder with the revision you intend to use.

item.title: ABAC: attribute-based access control
item.description: How ABAC works in Speedle Attribute-based access control (ABAC) uses properties of the subject, resource or request environment to determine access. In Speedle, SPDL conditions evaluate runtime attributes alongside the principal, action and resource. An application or trusted integration must collect those attributes and give them consistent names and types. For example, a role may establish that Alice is a reader, while a clearance attribute determines whether she may read a particular class of information.

item.title: Authorization Decisions
item.description: What is an authorization decision? Speedle evaluates a subject, action and resource within a service. The application must enforce the result. Treat an evaluation error or timeout separately from a normal Deny and fail closed. REST, gRPC and embedded Go APIs have different wire representations; use their respective contracts. Before running the examples Build ./bin/spctl, ./bin/speedle-pms and ./bin/speedle-ads using the quick start. Use Go 1.26 or later, Bash, curl and Python 3.

item.title: PBAC: policy-based access control
item.description: What PBAC means here Policy-based access control (PBAC) expresses authorization rules as managed policies instead of scattering permission checks across application code. Speedle+ uses the Speedle Policy Definition Language (SPDL), a Policy Management Service (PMS), and an Authorization Decision Service (ADS) or embedded evaluator. PBAC describes how rules are expressed and managed. RBAC describes role relationships; ABAC describes attribute conditions. A Speedle policy-based system can use both. From policy to enforcement Define the service, principal names, resource identifiers and supported actions.

item.title: Identity Domain
item.description: What is an identity domain? An identity domain (idd) is an explicit namespace for a principal. Two users named user1 can belong to different domains. The string is supplied by trusted integration code or a configured token asserter; it is not proof of authentication. Speedle does not infer or validate a provider’s tenant model merely from the domain name. Represent domains in policies and requests grant user user1 from github read book grant user user1 from IDCS.

item.title: Identity and IAM integration
item.description: Where Speedle fits in IAM Identity and access management (IAM) includes establishing identities, authenticating users, managing account lifecycles and controlling access. Speedle+ supplies an authorization engine within that architecture: it evaluates what an identified user, group or service may do. It is not a complete identity directory, login service or account-provisioning system. Responsibility Typical owner Accounts, credentials and login Identity provider and directory Trusted principal names, groups and attributes Application integration or token asserter Authorization and role policies Speedle Policy Management Service Access decision Speedle Authorization Decision Service or embedded evaluator Enforcing the decision on the actual resource Application or gateway Supply a trusted identity A trusted application can send explicit principals in the decision request.

item.title: Oracle Entitlements Server (OES) and Speedle
item.description: Why compare OES and Speedle? Oracle Entitlements Server (OES) and Speedle+ both address externalized, fine-grained authorization. Oracle’s OES architecture documentation describes centralized policy management and security modules that evaluate and enforce authorization policies. Speedle provides policy management and authorization decisions through its own services and APIs. The comparison is useful when reviewing an existing OES integration or evaluating an open-source authorization engine. Similar responsibilities do not make the products interchangeable.

item.title: Token asserter
item.description: What does a token asserter do? A configured asserter validates a token and returns explicit principals, including their identity domains. Speedle can then evaluate policies using those identities. A production implementation must validate the token’s signature or introspection result, issuer, audience, expiry and any provider-specific requirements. The webhook alone does not establish compatibility with arbitrary OAuth/OIDC tokens. The Token Assertion Plugin API uses integer errCode and an optional attribute object, not a typed attribute array.

The Policy Management Service (PMS) golang API is called to do policy management, and the Authorization Decision Service (ADS) golang API is called to do runtime authorization checks. item.title: XACML, SPDL and authorization architecture
item.description: What is the relationship to XACML? The eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML) is an OASIS access control standard defining policy and request/response concepts. Speedle+ uses its own Speedle Policy Definition Language (SPDL) and APIs. The OASIS XACML 3.0 specification is the reference for XACML behavior; this page explains architectural correspondences, not XACML conformance. Map the responsibilities XACML concept Responsibility Speedle+ correspondence PAP: Policy Administration Point Manage authorization policy Policy Management Service (PMS) PDP: Policy Decision Point Evaluate authorization requests Authorization Decision Service (ADS) or embedded evaluator PEP: Policy Enforcement Point Enforce a decision on an operation Application, gateway or integration calling Speedle PIP: Policy Information Point Supply attributes used by a decision Trusted application data and configured identity/attribute integrations; no claim of a built-in XACML PIP interface Speedle’s architecture page already describes the PAP/PDP correspondence.

item.title: Pluggable Storage
item.description: Built-in stores and extension contracts The standalone binaries register file, etcd and MongoDB implementations under pkg/store. Availability does not mean identical operational guarantees; review backend authentication, persistence, transaction and watch behavior for your deployment. The configuration below illustrates property names; running etcd/MongoDB deployments is outside this local example. A full backend implements pms.PolicyStoreManager: service, authorization-policy, role-policy and function management, snapshot reads, health checks, watch/stop, and close. ADS accepts the narrower PolicyStoreManagerADS read/watch interface.

item.title: Security
item.description: Protect both API transports Speedle’s standalone PMS and ADS expose REST and gRPC. Both now use the same --insecure, --cert, --key, --client-cert and --force-client-cert transport settings. Invalid certificates or trust configuration cause startup to fail; secure mode does not fall back to plaintext. TLS encrypts the connection and authenticates the server. To require authenticated clients, provide a client CA with --client-cert and set --force-client-cert=true. Without that flag, a configured CA validates a client certificate only when the client supplies one.

item.description: Overview The following two open source projects are used to process log messages, 1. https://github.com/sirupsen/logrus 2. https://github.com/natefinch/lumberjack Logrus is a structured logger for Go (golang), and completely API compatible with the golang standard library logger. Note that logrus doesn’t support log rotation, and it is exactly the reason why we introduce the second project lumberjack, which provides a rolling logger. item.title: Versions
item.description: Current development documentation These pages describe the current master source, not a frozen historical release. The current module requires Go 1.26 or later. The quick-start workflow verifies Go 1.26.10 and 1.27.3; those tested patch versions are not a promise that an old release has the same requirements. When upgrading, review the chosen commit and dependencies and repeat the integration checks for your store, transport and identity provider. Current standalone gRPC uses the same TLS/mTLS settings as REST and inherits its listening host unless --grpc-endpoint is supplied.

item.title: Custom Function
item.description: Why use a custom function? SPDL conditions can call a configured function when built-in operators or functions do not express the required rule. Speedle calls its REST endpoint with POST {"params":[...]} and expects {"result":...} or {"error":"..."}. Parameter order/types and the result type must match the condition. Function failures are evaluation errors; applications must fail closed. Start the local example This example accepts numeric values from 100 to 50000. Wrong parameter types or an empty parameter list return an HTTP error.

item.title: About Speedle
item.description: Speedle is an open source, fine-grained access control engine built to address authorization requirements in cloud-native applications. Speedle offers policy-driven access control that provides the ability to externalize authorization decisions to a policy engine that that can evaluate RBAC/ABAC policies for a given logged-in user, or on a process acting on behalf of a user. item.description: FAQs Speedle looks awesome! Who is it for? Speedle is an open source project for access management. You can embed it in your system as long as access control is required, such that you don’t have to hard code authorization policies in your code. Does the world need one more policy engine? Well, please spend 15 minutes on Quick Start steps. Then you will have the answer. Why not give a try?
